# Naḷakapāna Sutta (MN 68 (PTS MN i 462))

**ID:** MN 68 (PTS MN i 462)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Naḷakapāna Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** At Naḷakapāna
**PTS:** MN i 462
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Naḷakapāna Sutta* (MN 68; PTS MN i 462) is set in the Kosalan country at Naḷakapāna in the Palāsa Grove [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. It concerns a group of well-known clansmen who had gone forth into homelessness out of faith under the Buddha—including Anuruddha, Nandiya, Kimbila, and Bhagu [Freedman 1977; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2016]. In the discourse, the Buddha explains that those who practice do so not because of life failure, but because they aspire to higher freedom. He addresses why he declares the spiritual attainments and rebirth destinations of deceased disciples: rather than seeking admiration, display, or flattery, such declarations are intended to inspire other disciples across the four assemblies to emulate their example, arouse confidence, and overcome defilements [Matsuo 2015; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2018; Collett 2014]. The sutta also touches on abandoning the five mental hindrances, weariness, and discontent through meditative attainments (*jhāna*) [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Brahm 2014].
